clue.text: Favoured by decorators in Sheen ?

parts.note: Sheen looks like the London district, but read as a shiny finish it describes a type of paint decorators choose for a glossy coat

explanation.surface: A trade preference among house painters working in the Sheen area of London.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheen is a district of south-west London, so the capital letter makes it look like a place; read as lustre, it asks what decorators use to give a shine.
explanation.definitionFit: A high-lustre paint gives woodwork a shine, the kind of finish decorators reach for.

clue.text: French sleeve of the nineties

parts.note: the French word for a leg of lamb named the puffed leg-of-mutton sleeve fashionable in the 1890s

explanation.surface: A style of sleeve from France in the 1890s.
explanation.definitionFit: This leg-of-mutton style, wide at the shoulder and tight at the wrist, was fashionable in the 1890s.

clue.text: A slick form of modern transport ?

definitions.text: A slick form of modern transport ?

parts.words: A slick form of modern transport ?
parts.note: slick looks like smart, but an oil slick is what a wrecked petroleum-carrying ship may produce

explanation.surface: A smart, modern way of getting about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slick' suggests stylish, but read as a spill on the sea it points to the bulk ship that carries petroleum.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship built to carry petroleum in bulk is modern transport, and a spill from one makes a slick.

clue.text: Inventions of inventions ?

parts.note: the first inventions means made-up stories, the second means technological devices, so stories made up about gadgets and future science

explanation.surface: A puzzling question about devices that invent other devices.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word has two senses: fictions (made-up tales) about inventions (new machines and discoveries).
explanation.definitionFit: This genre is imaginative storytelling built around futuristic technology and discoveries.

clue.text: Hypothetical Pan's composer housed in Bavaria

parts.note: an is an archaic word for if, so 'ans' are hypotheticals, as in ifs and ans
J S Bach composed the secular cantata Phoebus and Pan

explanation.surface: The man who composed a supposed work about Pan was living in Bavaria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ifs and ans' is an old phrase for hypotheses; 'housed in Bavaria' defines a place where people are housed, a town in Bavaria.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a town in Franconia, in the German state of Bavaria.

clue.text: Lightly hand-over-hand to the highest point in time

definitions.text: Lightly hand-over-hand to the highest point in time

parts.words: Lightly hand-over-hand to the highest point in time
parts.note: lightly means in daylight; both clock hands lie over each other pointing straight up at the top of the dial, midday

explanation.surface: Climbing a rope hand over hand to the summit, with little effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hand-over-hand' looks like rope climbing; it is the clock's two hands overlapping at twelve, and 'Lightly' means in daylight, so twelve in the day.
explanation.definitionFit: At midday both clock hands point to twelve, the top of the face, in full daylight.

clue.text: Minnie, as you might say, ditched

definitions.text: Minnie, as you might say, ditched

parts.words: Minnie, as you might say, ditched
parts.note: Longfellow's heroine in Hiawatha, Minnie of the laughing water, minus her first name leaves a word for a sunken ditch used as a garden boundary

explanation.surface: Someone called Minnie has been dumped, to put it casually.
explanation.walkthrough: Hiawatha's bride in Longfellow's poem is Minnie plus a laughing word; drop the 'Minnie' and what remains is a ditch-and-wall boundary in English landscape gardens, so 'ditched' is the clue to the sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The garden feature is a boundary sunk in a trench, so it is literally a ditched fence.

clue.text: Where I was when I wasn't there, so to speak

definitions.text: Where I was when I wasn't there, so to speak

parts.words: Where I was when I wasn't there, so to speak
parts.note: the Latin word means elsewhere: a suspect's claim to have been somewhere other than the scene

explanation.surface: A puzzled person describing where they were while absent.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin original means 'elsewhere', the place you were when you were not at the crime scene.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a defence that the accused was elsewhere when the crime took place.

clue.text: The queen is in the herb garden

explanation.surface: Her Majesty is out among the herbs.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen Artemisia of Caria built the Mausoleum for her husband; her name is borne by the plant genus that includes wormwood, mugwort and tarragon.
explanation.definitionFit: Artemisia was a queen of Caria; the same name is a genus of aromatic plants such as wormwood and tarragon.

clue.text: It's heavenly !

parts.note: heavenly is praise for something wonderful, and also literally beyond the earth

explanation.surface: An exclamation of delight.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means wonderful and also, literally, belonging beyond our planet, as heaven does.

clue.text: Drink measures, about one quarter, for Fisher's assistants

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the drink measures are placed around the other letters

parts.note: a gill is a small measure of liquor, a quarter of a pint
one is the Roman numeral I
E, east, is one of the four quarters of the compass

explanation.surface: Someone measuring out drinks, roughly a quarter each, for the helpers of a man who fishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarter' tempts as a quarter of a gill, but here it is a compass point, E.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland these are the attendants who help a sportsman fishing or shooting.

clue.text: He conducts an alphabetical questionnaire, d'you see ?

definitions.text: He conducts an alphabetical questionnaire, d'you see ?

parts.words: He conducts an alphabetical questionnaire, d'you see ?
parts.note: the eye specialist asks a patient to read rows of letters off a chart and keeps asking whether they can see them

explanation.surface: A man running a survey in alphabetical order checks whether you understand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'd'you see' sounds like 'understand?' but is the literal question an eye examiner asks over a letter chart.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye doctor tests vision with a chart of letters, asking what the patient can see.

clue.text: Teach musicians for the militia

parts.note: to teach is to train
a group of musicians is a band

explanation.surface: Instruct a group of players to perform for the soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: This was a historical company of citizen soldiers, a local militia in Tudor and Stuart England.

clue.text: For love into the mire back I go ? For hate

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

indicators.note: into means the I goes inside the reversed mire
back means the word for the mire is read backwards

parts.note: mire is mud

explanation.surface: A lover sinking back into the mud, then asking whether this is for hatred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns MUD into DUM; 'into' puts I inside it to give DIUM, after O.
explanation.definitionFit: This means intense hatred or general loathing directed at someone.

clue.text: 1914 leg show

parts.note: around 1914 hemlines rose just far enough to show the joint at the bottom of the leg, which was then considered daring

explanation.surface: A risque display of legs on stage in 1914.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leg show' suggests a revue, but the clue means how much leg a 1914 skirt revealed: only the bit above the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Fashion of the period first lifted skirts to reveal the joint joining foot and leg.

clue.text: Making progress putting people in the red ?

explanation.surface: Getting ahead by driving others into debt.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is going forward; the other is paying out money in advance, which puts the recipients in debt (in the red).
explanation.definitionFit: Going forward means making progress; lending money up front leaves borrowers in debt.

clue.text: Products of the hours a dial shows

definitions.text: Products of the hours a dial shows

parts.words: Products of the hours a dial shows
parts.note: a sundial only shows the hours when the sun shines, the very time when, as the proverb says, farmers make their dried grass

explanation.surface: What is produced in the time shown on a clock face.
explanation.walkthrough: The dial is a sundial, which records only sunny hours; 'make hay while the sun shines', so the stacks of dried grass are what those hours produce.
explanation.definitionFit: Piles of dried grass are built on sunny days, the only hours a sundial marks.

clue.text: Utterly low of a woman

parts.note: utterly is a play on utter, to sing out: the voice a woman utters at its lowest is this one

explanation.surface: Someone condemning a woman's behaviour as completely base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utterly low' sounds like contempt, but it means low in what she utters: the lowest female singing voice.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the deepest female singing voice, below mezzo-soprano.

clue.text: This appendix is not for bookworms, though

definitions.text: This appendix is not for bookworms, though

parts.words: This appendix is not for bookworms, though
parts.note: the appendix is the body's worm-shaped organ, not the end section of a book that a bookworm would read

explanation.surface: A remark that a book's appendix will not interest keen readers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appendix' looks like the back of a book, but it is the worm-shaped one in the gut; 'though' admits the irony that it is shaped like a worm.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means worm-shaped and is the anatomical name for the gut's appendix.

clue.text: Nag, Kipling's, was in this order

definitions.text: Nag, Kipling's, was in this order

parts.words: Nag, Kipling's, was in this order
parts.note: Nag is the cobra in Kipling's Rikki-Tikki-Tavi, so the order meant is the zoological grouping of snakes

explanation.surface: Kipling's old horse belonged to a particular ranking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nag' suggests a horse; in Kipling's Jungle Book story it is the cobra fought by the mongoose, and 'order' is a taxonomic rank.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an old zoological name for the order of snakes, to which cobras belong.

clue.text: Like my halls of dream

parts.note: the song from The Bohemian Girl runs 'I dreamt that I dwelt in marble halls', so the halls are made of polished stone

explanation.surface: A wistful description of the rooms of one's imagination.
explanation.walkthrough: The allusion is to Balfe's popular Victorian song 'I Dreamt I Dwelt in Marble Halls'.
explanation.definitionFit: Halls built of veined polished stone, as in the dreamt halls of the song.

clue.text: Greek settlement one found in St Columba's isle

indicators.note: found in means the one is placed inside the island's name

parts.note: Saint Columba founded his monastery on the Scottish island of Iona
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A Greek colony discovered on the island of the Irish saint.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the region of Greek colonies on the west coast of Asia Minor.

clue.text: Rembrandt's watch

parts.note: Rembrandt's most famous group portrait is known by a title naming a dark-hours watch, and a watch is a period of the dark hours

explanation.surface: The timepiece belonging to the Dutch painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'watch' looks like a timepiece, but Rembrandt's painting of the civic guard is famous under a title meaning the after-dark watch.
explanation.definitionFit: Rembrandt's great militia painting is popularly titled after this period of darkness.

clue.text: More than the iceberg's tip showing up-may have a crest

indicators.note: showing up in a down clue means the letters are read upwards, backwards
more than the tip means a little more than the visible 'berg' part of the word iceberg is taken

explanation.surface: Rather more than the tip of an iceberg is visible, with a crest of foam.
explanation.walkthrough: Take a little more than the 'berg' at the end of iceberg, EBERG, and 'showing up' turns it to give the diving bird; 'tip' completes the phrase 'more than the tip'.
explanation.definitionFit: The great crested grebe is a familiar water bird with a crest of head feathers.

clue.text: Concrete terms ? Hostile ones

explanation.surface: A question about specific language, answered with angry language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concrete' is used for its physical sense: concrete is solid, so terms made of it are firm ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Solid like concrete gives firm expressions; the phrase also means angry, harsh remarks exchanged in a quarrel.

clue.text: Youth who flourishes by graft

explanation.surface: A young person who succeeds through hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'graft' looks like British slang for hard work; it is the horticultural joining of a cutting to a rootstock.
explanation.definitionFit: A young heir of a noble family, and a shoot cut for grafting onto another plant.

clue.text: Hard water is not necessarily this

definitions.text: Hard water is not necessarily this

parts.words: Hard water is not necessarily this
parts.note: hard water means water rich in minerals, but read literally hard water is frozen, which mineral-rich water need not be

explanation.surface: A remark that limescale-laden water need not be chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard water' looks like the chemist's term for mineral-rich supply; taken literally it is frozen, and the clue notes hard tap water is not necessarily freezing.
explanation.definitionFit: Frozen water is solid, chilled to freezing, which mineral-laden tap water need not be.

clue.text: The German siren is learning to go with the French one

parts.note: lore is accumulated learning
le is French for the
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A German temptress is studying, together with a French one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the French one' reads as a second siren, but it gives LE (French 'the') and I.
explanation.definitionFit: In German legend, a maiden on a Rhine rock lures boatmen to their doom with song.

clue.text: Notes that neigh — almost hiss

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the word is left off

parts.note: hiss stands for the birds that hiss, farmyard geese

explanation.surface: Musical notes that whinny, and very nearly hiss.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the plural of the note G and a child's word for horses (gee-gees), which neigh; geese hiss, and 'almost' trims the final E.
explanation.definitionFit: The letters spell a plural of the note G and also horses in nursery talk, which whinny.

clue.text: Helped to alight by Will

explanation.surface: Assisted off a carriage by a man named Will.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' looks like a man's name; it is a testament, by which property is passed to heirs.
explanation.definitionFit: A passenger given a hand off a coach; also property passed on to heirs through a testament.
